steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
At a high level, a Transformer is a sequence-to-sequence model built almost entirely around “attention” rather than recurrence (RNNs) or convolution.  Here’s the conceptual flow:

1. Input Embedding + Positional Encoding  
   • Each token (word, subword, etc.) is mapped to a continuous d-dimensional vector.  
   • Since attention alone doesn’t know about word order, we add a fixed or learned positional encoding to each embedding so the model can tell “this comes before that.”

2. Stacked Encoder Layers  
   Each encoder layer has two main sub-layers, each followed by a residual (skip) connection and layer-normalization:  
   a. Multi-Head Self-Attention  
     – For each position in the input, compute three vectors: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) as linear projections of the embedding.  
     – Compute attention weights by taking the dot-product Q·Kᵀ (scaled by √dₖ), applying softmax to get a distribution over all positions, and then weighting the V vectors.  
     – Repeat this in H “heads” (different projection matrices) so the model can attend to different types of relationships in parallel.  
     – Concatenate the H results and linearly project back to the model dimension.  
   b. Position-Wise Feed-Forward Network  
     – A small two-layer fully connected network applied independently at each position:  
       FFN(x) = max(0, xW₁ + b₁)W₂ + b₂  

3. Decoder (for sequence-to-sequence tasks)  
   Like the encoder but with three sub-layers per block:  
   a. Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention (prevents each position from “seeing” future positions)  
   b. Multi-Head Cross-Attention over the encoder’s outputs (queries come from the decoder, keys/values from the encoder)  
   c. Position-Wise Feed-Forward Network  

4. Final Linear + Softmax (for generation/classification)  
   • In a language-modeling or translation setting, the decoder’s top layer projects each position back into the vocabulary space and applies softmax to produce a probability distribution over the next token.

Why it works so well  
– Self-attention lets every position directly “look at” every other position in the sequence (capturing long-range dependencies in a single layer).  
– Multi-head attention captures multiple kinds of relationships simultaneously.  
– Fully parallelizable (no step-by-step recurrence), so training on long sequences is much faster on modern hardware.  
– Residual connections + layer norms help training stability and gradient flow.

In essence, a Transformer “computes context” by letting each word dynamically attend to all others, layers that process and re-process those contextualized representations, and then (in a decoder) uses both self- and cross-attention to generate or classify outputs.
